title: Infections in HCT and Cellular Therapy Recipients

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman was reviewed with a 3-week history of fevers and a 1-week history of painful skin nodules. She was known to have a persistent neutropenia following an allogeneic stem cell transplant 4 weeks earlier for relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She had been taking levofloxacin, voriconazole, valaciclovir, and trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis; the levofloxacin had been switched to intravenous cefepime 3 weeks earlier, but her symptoms had progressed. On examination, her temperature was 103°F (39.4°C), her blood pressure was 110/68 mmHg, her heart rate was 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturations 98% on room air. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. There were multiple subcutaneous purplish popular and nodular lesions of various sizes scattered throughout her extremities, her neck, and her chest. Some of the lesions had central necrosis. She had pedal onychomycosis. Investigations: Total white cell count 0.2 ×109 /L (4–10) Absolute neutrophil count 0.0 ×109 /L (2–8) Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL (13–17) Platelets 43 ×109 /L (150–400) eGFR>60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Blood cultures at admission were negative, but repeat blood cultures at the point of review 3 weeks later were positive for a mold.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fusarium solani Fusarium are species of mold that may cause disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients. It tends to be more resistant to the azole antifungals than Aspergillus species but sensitive to amphotericin. Disseminated fusariosis may be identified through positive blood cultures. The typical clinical picture is as described in a patient with prolonged (>10 days) neutropenia, persistent fevers, widespread skin lesions that evolve rapidly, and blood cultures growing a mold. Unlike aspergillosis, blood cultures are commonly positive. Mortality rates are high even with appropriate antifungals and immunotherapy such as G-CSF . Because the pathogen identified is a mold, Candida tropicalis, Histoplasma capsulatum, and Cryptococcus neoformans would not be the answer, as they appear as yeast forms in the human body. However, these pathogens can cause disseminated nodular skin lesions in immunocompromised patients. Aspergillus fumigatus is not the correct answer, as voriconazole is usually effective prophylaxis against invasive aspergillus infections, and aspergillus rarely is identified in blood cultures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q39

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with chronic myelogenous leukemia received an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Her course was complicated by multiple episodes of graft-versus-host disease. She received courses of methylprednisolone. She was on maintenance immunosuppression with cyclosporine. On day 132, she developed fever and patchy pulmonary infiltrates and rapidly progressed into respiratory failure. She was intubated and underwent bronchoscopy. Branched hyphae were noted on the wet mount from the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid. The patient was commenced on liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg daily). Four days later the laboratory reported that the BAL culture grew Scedosporium apiospermum. The patient continued having fevers, and her respiratory status was not improving.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Increase the dose of amphotericin B to 10 mg/kg daily

questions.explanation: Switch to voriconazole Scedosporium apiospermum is resistant to amphotericin B and the echinocandins. Voriconazole is the treatment of choice. Posaconazole may be used as an alternative agent. In contrast to Scedosporium apiospermum, Scedosporium prolificans (now called Lomentospora prolificans) is resistant to all antifungals. Combination treatment with amphotericin B and echinocandins or terbinafine may be of benefit due to the potential synergistic activity in L. prolificans infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q30

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of diarrhea and shortness of breath. She had experienced bloody diarrhea and associated abdominal cramps, along with a dry cough but had not had any hemoptysis, chest pain, fevers, chills, or night sweats. She had relapsed Hodgkin’s lymphoma postallogeneic stem cell transplant 2 months ago, complicated by graft versus host disease (GVHD) of the gut, skin, and lungs. She had been treated with prednisone and tacrolimus, and the GVHD was felt to be under control. She was also taking trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole, levofloxacin, aciclovir, and voriconazole prophylaxis. She denied sick contacts and lived in an urban area. On examination, her temperature was 37.1°C, her blood pressure was 110/58 mmHg, her heart rate was 115 beats/ min, respiratory rate 24 breaths/minute, O 2 saturation 92% on 6 L/minute oxygen. She had pale conjunctivae. Respiratory examination revealed diffuse crackles bilaterally but no rhonchi or wheezes. Her abdomen was soft with mild diffuse tenderness to palpation and normal bowel sounds. There was 1+ pedal edema, and hyperpigmented areas on the arms/legs at sites of prior GVHD of the skin. Investigations: Total white cell count 3.0 ×109 /L Absolute neutrophil count 1.6 ×109 /L Hemoglobin 8 g/dL Platelets 98 ×109/L Urea, creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits Blood cultures: no growth at 48 hours C. difficile PCR negative Stool culture and stool ova and parasites negative CXR: bilateral interstitial infiltrates, no consolidation, no effusions CT abdomen/pelvis with and without contrast revealed diffuse colitis, no lymphadenopathy, no abscesses
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus Varicella may cause pneumonitis with hypoxemia in immunocompromised patients and may also cause gastrointestinal manifestations. However, the patient is on aciclovir, which is effective prophylaxis for varicella. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes both colitis and pneumonitis, among other manifestations. Infiltrates on imaging are usually interstitial, and diagnosis is made via CMV PCR of the blood in addition to bronchoscopy with positive transbronchial biopsy. CMV colitis may be associated with negative CMV PCR, so diagnosis would be through sigmoidoscopy with biopsy of the colon to look for CMV viral inclusions or positive immunostain on pathology. Aciclovir is not effective at preventing CMV . Strongyloides can cause both pneumonitis and gastroenteritis in immunocompromised patients, but the stool ova and parasite test is negative, and it is less common in transplant recipients who are not foreign-born or who reside in urban areas. Clostridioides difficile may cause colitis, but C. difficile PCR test is negative and has a very high sensitivity. In addition, C. difficile does not cause pneumonitis. Pneumocystis jirovecii may cause hypoxemia with interstitial pulmonary infiltrates in immunocompromised patients but does not cause colitis. In addition, this patient is on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, rendering pneumocystis pneumonia even less likely.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q25

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with a 2-day history of fever and chills, dyspnea, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Five months earlier she underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for myelodysplastic syndrome. She was taking trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, aciclovir, prednisone, and cyclosporine. Investigations: CXR: infiltrate in the left lower lobe
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae The patient is 5 months out from a stem cell transplant and presents with a lobar pneumonia. Although she is immunocompromised, she is on Pneumocystis prophylaxis and does not present with interstitial lung disease. CMV pneumonia would also be unlikely without a diffuse pneumonitis on imaging, and she would require histopathology with positive CMV staining to make the diagnosis. RSV pneumonia would normally present with bilateral asymmetric infiltrates and Candida spp. rarely cause pneumonia. The correct answer is therefore pneumococcal pneumonia as this patient is at risk for pneumococcal pneumonia, and a lower lobe infiltrate would fit the classic description.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q4

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of shortness of breath and dry cough. There was no history of fever, hemoptysis, or coryzal symptoms. She had no sick contacts and no recent travel outside of the United States. She was 60 days postallogeneic stem cell transplant for acute myelogenous leukemia. She had previously had Stevens–Johnson syndrome due to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. She was taking levofloxacin, valaciclovir, voriconazole, and inhaled pentamidine. On examination, her temperature was 37.2°C, blood pressure was 132/65 mmHg, heart rate 105 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/minute, oxygen saturations 88% on 2LPM of O 2. Cardiovascular exam was unremarkable; respiratory exam revealed faint bilateral crackles. There was no pedal edema, and the rest of the exam was unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 1.4 ×109/L Absolute neutrophil count 0.8 ×109 /L Hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL Platelets 98 ×109 /L eGFR >60 mL/min per 1.73 m2 LDH 340 U/L Blood cultures: no growth at 48 hours CXR: diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae, although can cause pneumonia in transplant recipients, would be unlikely given the levofloxacin prophylaxis, which is effective treatment for both of these pathogens. Typical findings on X-ray would be consolidations. Pulmonary aspergillosis would be unusual given the patient is on voriconazole prophylaxis, and typical findings on chest X-ray tend to be cavitations with aircrescent sign or nodules rather than interstitial infiltrates. MERS coronavirus can cause hypoxemia and interstitial infiltrates on chest radiography; however, the patient has not traveled to a part of the world affected by MERS coronavirus, such as the Middle East. Although the patient is receiving inhaled pentamidine for pneumocystis prophylaxis, this is not as effective as trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, and breakthrough infections have been reported. Thus the correct answer is Pneumocystis jirovecii.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q25

questions.question: In an allogeneic HSCT recipient, name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens you would consider for prophylaxis in the pre-engraftment and post-engraftment periods and an agent for each. This patient goes on to develop graft-versus-host disease.
questions.question_raw: In an allo-HSCT recipient, name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens you would consider for prophylaxis for the pre-engraftment and post-engraftment period and an agent for each. This patient goes on to develop GVHD.

parts.text: Name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens you would consider for prophylaxis for the pre-engraftment and post-engraftment period and an agent for each.
Name one bacterial pathogen you would consider prophylaxis for, given GVHD.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens you would consider for prophylaxis for the pre-engraftment and post-engraftment period and an agent for each
Name one bacterial pathogen you would consider prophylaxis for (given GVHD).

questions.model_answer:
a) Pre-engraftment (neutropenic phase): (1) Gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas -> fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 500 mg daily); (2) Candida -> fluconazole 400 mg daily; plus HSV -> acyclovir/valacyclovir in seropositive patients. Post-engraftment: (1) Pneumocystis jirovecii -> TMP-SMX; (2) CMV -> letermovir prophylaxis (or valganciclovir/pre-emptive strategy); mould-active azole (posaconazole/voriconazole) if ongoing GVHD.
b) Streptococcus pneumoniae (encapsulated organisms) -> penicillin (or TMP-SMX/macrolide); patients with chronic GVHD are functionally asplenic/hyposplenic and at high risk of invasive pneumococcal disease.
questions.beyond_mandell: Regimen specifics (letermovir, levofloxacin dosing) reflect ASTCT/IDSA and ECIL HSCT prophylaxis guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-engraftment: yeast - Fluconazole; Bacteria (GNB, especially Pseudomonas) - Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin. Post-engraftment: Pneumocystis jirovecii - Septra; CMV - Valganciclovir. GVHD: S. pneumoniae (encapsulated pathogens).

questions.question: For posaconazole prophylaxis, name three groups for which there is RCT data demonstrating decreased mortality and invasive fungal infections.

parts.text: For posaconazole prophylaxis, name three groups for which there is RCT data demonstrating decreased mortality and invasive fungal infections.

parts_raw.text: For posaconazole prophylaxis, name three groups for which there is RCT data demonstrating decreased mortality and invasive fungal infections.

questions.model_answer: (1) Patients with prolonged neutropenia from remission-induction chemotherapy for AML or myelodysplastic syndrome (Cornely et al., NEJM 2007 — fewer invasive fungal infections and lower all-cause mortality vs fluconazole/itraconazole). (2) Allogeneic HSCT recipients with graft-versus-host disease receiving intensive immunosuppression (Ullmann et al., NEJM 2007 — fewer invasive aspergillosis cases and fewer fungal-related deaths vs fluconazole). (3) More broadly, high-risk hematologic malignancy patients with anticipated prolonged neutropenia, the populations in which these two RCTs established mortality benefit.
questions.beyond_mandell: Cornely NEJM 2007;356:348 and Ullmann NEJM 2007;356:335 are the pivotal RCTs.

parts.text: What prophylaxis will you offer if HSV IgG positive?
What prophylaxis will you offer if VZV IgG positive?

parts_raw.text: What prophylaxis will you offer if HSV IgG positive?

questions.model_answer:
a) HSV IgG positive: acyclovir or valacyclovir from conditioning through engraftment/resolution of mucositis (~30 days); commonly continued given overlap with VZV prophylaxis.
b) VZV IgG positive: acyclovir/valacyclovir prophylaxis continued for ~1 year post-transplant (longer while immunosuppressed/GVHD), stopped around the time of VZV vaccination once off immunosuppression.
c) Hepatitis B (HBsAg negative, HBsAb positive, HBcAb negative): no antiviral prophylaxis needed - this is a vaccine-immune pattern with no evidence of prior infection.
d) Toxoplasma IgG positive: no dedicated toxoplasmosis agent; TMP-SMX given for PJP prophylaxis also provides toxoplasma prophylaxis. Consider toxoplasma PCR monitoring/dedicated prophylaxis only in high-risk allogeneic recipients.
questions.beyond_mandell: Serology-driven prophylaxis (HBcAb-negative interpretation, toxoplasma coverage by TMP-SMX) per ASTCT/ECIL guidance.

cohort_answer.text: HSV IgG+: Prophylaxis with (Val)Acyclovir until 1 month post transplant. VZV IgG+: Valacyclovir until day prior to VZV vaccination (no sooner than 2 years post-transplant or later if still immunosuppressed). Hepatitis B (immune pattern): Nothing. Toxoplasma IgG+: Nothing unless very high risk

parts_raw.text: HSV IgG positive
VZV IgG positive
Hepatitis B HBsAg negative, HBsAb positive, HBcAb negative

questions.model_answer:
a) HSV IgG positive: acyclovir/valacyclovir prophylaxis from conditioning through engraftment/mucositis resolution (~30 days), often extended given VZV coverage overlap.
b) VZV IgG positive: acyclovir/valacyclovir prophylaxis continued ~1 year (longer while on immunosuppression or with GVHD), stopped around VZV vaccination once off immunosuppression.
c) Hepatitis B (HBsAg neg, HBsAb pos, HBcAb neg): no prophylaxis - vaccine-immune pattern, no prior infection or reactivation risk.
d) Toxoplasma IgG positive: no dedicated agent; TMP-SMX given for PJP prophylaxis also covers toxoplasmosis. Consider toxoplasma PCR monitoring in high-risk allogeneic recipients.

cohort_answer.text: HSV IgG positive: Acyclovir prophylaxis for at least 1 year post transplant (some institutions until immune restoration 2 years with no ongoing IS or cGVHD); AHS guide: valacyclovir accepted until 1-month post-transplant, controversial until 3 months (possibly useful for HSV seropositive recipients with HSV seronegative donors); irrelevant for patients on VZV prophylaxis, who get valacyclovir anyway. VZV IgG positive: Acyclovir prophylaxis at least 1 year post transplant; use valacyclovir followed by VZV vaccination (effective for eliminating post-herpetic neuralgia); give valacyclovir until VZV vaccination at 24 months post-transplant in patients free of active cGVHD and off immunosuppressive therapy, or >=3 months after discontinuation of immunosuppressive therapy when cGVHD inactive. Hepatitis B (HBsAg neg, HBsAb pos, HBcAb neg): Nothing - patient was previously immune and has no evidence of infection. Toxoplasma IgG positive: Generally no specific prophylaxis for toxo in HSCT but patient would be receiving PJP prophylaxis for at least 6 months post-transplant

parts.text: List FIVE risk factors for CMV infection in hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
Describe prophylactic therapy and pre-emptive therapy.
How is ganciclovir cleared and in what population is dose adjustment required?
List THREE alternate medications that can be used with mutations in UL97 and ONE alternate medication that can be used with mutations in UL54.

parts_raw.text: List FIVE risk factors for CMV infection in hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
Describe prophylactic therapy and pre-emptive therapy.
How is ganciclovir cleared and in what population is dose adjustment required?
List THREE alternate medications that can be used with mutations in UL97 and ONE alternate medication that can be used with mutations in UL54.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Seropositive recipient (R+; D+/R+ or D-/R+ is the high-risk group in HSCT). (2) HLA mismatch between donor and recipient. (3) Use of T-lymphocyte-depleting strategies (antithymocyte globulin or alemtuzumab). (4) Umbilical cord stem cell transplant into a seropositive recipient. (5) Graft-versus-host disease requiring steroid therapy (HLA-haploidentical HSCT is a further factor).
b) Prophylaxis: antiviral is given to all at-risk recipients regardless of viral detection, for a defined period after transplant (often to ~day 100), frequently followed by a pre-emptive strategy once prophylaxis stops. Pre-emptive therapy: serial quantitative virologic monitoring (qPCR/antigenemia) is performed and antiviral treatment is started only when a predetermined threshold of replication is reached, continuing until resolution or significant reduction of virus.
c) Ganciclovir is not appreciably metabolized and is excreted almost unchanged into the urine; dosing therefore depends on renal function, so dose adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment.
d) UL97 (impaired phosphorylation): (1) foscarnet, (2) cidofovir, (3) letermovir (maribavir also active). UL54 (altered DNA polymerase, cross-resistant to GCV/foscarnet/cidofovir): letermovir (terminase inhibitor, activity independent of UL54).

questions.question: Invasive aspergillosis in a bone marrow transplant patient.
questions.question_raw: Q56 2023 Part 2. Invasive aspergillosis in a BMT patient. (FUNGAL)

parts.text: Give three radiographic findings consistent with invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
What is the preferred treatment?
With acute kidney injury and prolonged QTc, what is the best treatment option?

parts_raw.text: 3 radiographic findings consistent with IPA
Preferred treatment
AKI and prolonged QTc, what is best treatment option

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Halo sign (low-attenuation rim around a nodule; early finding). (2) Air-crescent sign (late, with neutrophil recovery). (3) Dense nodular infiltrates and/or pleural-based, wedge-shaped densities or cavitation.
b) Voriconazole (alternatives: liposomal amphotericin B or isavuconazole).
c) Isavuconazole – it shortens the QTc and requires no renal dose adjustment (avoids the QT prolongation of voriconazole and the nephrotoxicity of amphotericin B; IV voriconazole's cyclodextrin vehicle is also a concern in renal failure).

cohort_answer.text:
3 radiographic findings (Mandell IPA CT findings): diffuse nodular infiltrates; halo sign (density surrounded by a ring of low-attenuation, early sign); classic pleural-based wedge density (early, less common); cavity lesions (late); pleural effusions; 'crescent sign' (nodular lesion that cavitates).
Preferred treatment (IDSA Aspergillus Guidelines): Voriconazole. Alternates: ampho B liposomal, isavuconazole, or other lipid formulations of ampho B. Echinocandin monotherapy not recommended.
Best option with AKI/QTc prolongation: For AKI - Voriconazole (oral) or isavuconazole do not require dose adjustment; IV voriconazole contains cyclodextrin which theoretically accumulates renally, but not clinically demonstrated; IDSA states relative benefits/risks of IV voriconazole in renal failure should be individualized. For QTc prolongation: Isavuconazole, which 'shortens the QTc, clinical significance unclear'.

parts.text: List the organisms possibly involved.
Treatment.
Further investigations.

parts_raw.text: A) List the organisms possibly involved
B) Treatment
C) Further investigations

questions.model_answer:
a) Bacterial: community-acquired pneumonia incl. atypicals, Nocardia, NTM/Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Fungal: invasive aspergillosis, Mucorales, Pneumocystis jirovecii. Viral: CMV pneumonitis, respiratory viruses (RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus). Parasitic: disseminated Strongyloides. Non-infectious mimics: GVHD/bronchiolitis obliterans, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, PTLD, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
b) Empiric broad-spectrum antibacterials (ceftriaxone + azithromycin for CAP; extend to antipseudomonal beta-lactam if neutropenic); add TMP-SMX +/- steroids if PJP suspected; mould-active azole (voriconazole) if aspergillosis suspected; ganciclovir if CMV pneumonitis. Tailor to results.
c) CT chest; respiratory viral and atypical PCR on NP swab; bronchoscopy with BAL for bacterial/fungal/AFB culture, PJP and Legionella PCR, galactomannan, and CMV; blood CMV PCR and serum/BAL galactomannan; consider lung biopsy for peripheral nodules or if BAL non-diagnostic (also assesses PTLD/GVHD).

cohort_answer.text: A) Invasive aspergillosis, mucormycosis; CAP including atypicals; viral pneumonia including CMV pneumonitis; PJP; Nocardia; NTM, TB; disseminated Strongyloides. Non-infectious: GVHD, PTLD, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia. B) Depends if also neutropenic; empiric Ceftriaxone + Azithro for CAP; +/- Septra and steroids for PJP if not already on ppx and acutely unwell; +/- voriconazole for aspergillus if not already on ppx. C) Respiratory viral PCR on NP aspirate; CT chest; bronchoscopy with BAL (tissue to histopathology); CMV tissue to assess invasive disease; PJP and legionella PCR, AFB/fungal/bacterial culture; +/- lung biopsy if peripheral nodule (also for PTLD).

questions.question: A patient is 30 days out from an allogeneic transplant complicated by severe Candida mucositis treated with fluconazole, and now has increasing liver enzymes.
questions.question_raw: A patient is 30 days out from an allogeneic transplant which was complicated by severe candida mucositis and treated with fluconazole. Now has increasing LFTs.

parts.text: What is the probable cause?
What would you do with this patient now? Justify your answer.

parts_raw.text: What is the probable cause?
What would you do with this patient now? Justify your answer

questions.model_answer:
a) The most probable cause is fluconazole (azole) hepatotoxicity. The key differential is hepatosplenic (chronic disseminated) candidiasis, which classically becomes manifest during recovery from neutropenia around engraftment; other considerations include sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/VOD, acute GVHD, viral hepatitis (CMV, HSV, HHV6, hepatitis viruses), and other hepatotoxic drugs (calcineurin inhibitors, methotrexate, TMP-SMX).
b) (1) Investigate: check LFT pattern and trend, and obtain cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI/US of liver and spleen) looking for the characteristic small abscesses of hepatosplenic candidiasis, plus blood cultures for yeast. (2) Stop the fluconazole given the transaminitis and switch antifungal cover to an echinocandin (or a lipid-formulation amphotericin B), which are the recommended agents for chronic disseminated/hepatosplenic candidiasis and avoid ongoing azole hepatotoxicity; if an azole is later required, posaconazole is better tolerated. (3) Exclude the competing diagnoses (viral serologies/PCR, review of hepatotoxic drugs, assess for VOD/GVHD). Justification: fever and abnormal LFTs long after culture-negativity are typical of hepatosplenic candidiasis, which requires prolonged echinocandin/LFAMB therapy with later step-down to fluconazole once stable and non-neutropenic; adjuvant corticosteroids may help prolonged disabling fever.
questions.beyond_mandell: Attribution of the transaminitis specifically to fluconazole hepatotoxicity and the post-HSCT differential (VOD, GVHD, viral hepatitis) rest on general HSCT/drug-toxicity knowledge, not this Mandell slice.

cohort_answer.text: A) Fluconazole-induced hepatotoxicity. DDX: hepatosplenic candidiasis (manifests at engraftment, median presentation 2-3 weeks post-HSCT if no ppx); CMV/VZV/EBV/HHV6/HSV/HBV (HSV highest risk pre-engraftment, usually on ppx); hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome/VOD (elevated bili, hepatomegaly/RUQ pain, sudden weight gain, needs biopsy; risk factors liver dysfunction pre-tx, poorly matched donor, MTX for GVHD ppx); acute GVHD; other drugs (calcineurin inhibitor, methotrexate, TMP-SMX). B) CT abdomen/pelvis to work up hepatosplenic candidiasis; blood cultures for yeast; once cultures obtained, stop fluconazole, start echinocandin; if azole required use Posaconazole (reduced transaminitis); IDSA alternative: IV echinocandin or IV lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg daily; start empiric acyclovir for HSV if not on ppx; trend liver enzymes; look for non-infectious causes; consider esophageal brushings for yeast culture/sensitivity, Herpesviridae viral load.

questions.question: Name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens and an appropriate prophylaxis regimen for each: bacteria (mainly Gram-negative including Pseudomonas); fungus; Herpesviridae.
questions.question_raw: Name 2 pathogens or groups of pathogens and an appropriate prophylaxis regimen for each: Bacteria (mainly gram negative including Pseudomonas); Fungus; Herpesviridae

parts.text: Bacteria.
Fungus.
Herpesviridae.

parts_raw.text: Bacteria
Fungus
Herpesviridae

questions.model_answer:
a) Bacteria (Gram-negative incl. Pseudomonas): fluoroquinolone prophylaxis during profound/prolonged neutropenia - levofloxacin 500 mg daily (or ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID) until engraftment; prolonged penicillin/TMP-SMX only for pneumococcal prevention in allogeneic recipients with chronic GVHD.
b) Fungus: Candida -> fluconazole 400 mg daily until engraftment; mould-active azole (posaconazole, covers Mucorales; or voriconazole) for high-risk post-engraftment GVHD; Pneumocystis jirovecii -> TMP-SMX 1 DS daily or 3x/week.
c) Herpesviridae: HSV/VZV -> acyclovir 800 mg BID (or valacyclovir) in seropositive patients, ~1 year for VZV; CMV -> letermovir prophylaxis (or ganciclovir/valganciclovir, pre-emptive strategy) through day 100.
questions.beyond_mandell: Agent choices (letermovir, posaconazole for Mucorales, FQ dosing) per ASTCT/IDSA and ECIL HSCT prophylaxis guidelines.

cohort_answer.text: Bacteria: FQ ppx for high-risk patients with prolonged/profound neutropenia - Levofloxacin 500mg daily or ciprofloxacin 500mg BID, until end of neutropenia/engraftment or last chemo dose; prolonged ppx (>100d post-HSCT) only for S. pneumo prevention in allogeneic recipients with chronic GVHD on chemo. Fungus: Candida ppx for all HSCT or intensive remission-induction/salvage chemo for acute leukemia - Fluconazole 400mg daily (until engraftment or 75 days post-transplant, or until immunosuppression discontinued for secondary ppx); mold ppx (Aspergillus, Mucor) for highest-risk HSCT post-engraftment with GVHD - Voriconazole (no mucor coverage) or Posaconazole (covers mucor, liquid 200mg TID or delayed release 300mg BID day1 then 300mg daily); PJP ppx - TMP/SMX 1 DS tab daily, 1 SS tab daily, or 1 DS tab 3x/week. Herpesviridae: HSV ppx with acyclovir 800mg BID in all HSV+ HSCT/acute leukemia induction patients, until engraftment/resolution of mucositis (~30d), extended to 1 year for secondary ppx; CMV ppx for CMV r+ or r-/d+ with CMV safe blood products, Ganciclovir/Valganciclovir for 100d post-HSCT or Letermovir; VZV ppx for VZV r+ with Acyclovir or Valacyclovir 500mg BID for 1 year post-HSCT.

questions.question: A woman 3 weeks post-bone marrow transplant, known cytomegalovirus-positive and herpes simplex virus-positive, presents with acute respiratory illness and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows 3+ HSV. Name 3 possible causes other than HSV.
questions.question_raw: Q11 (2007). Woman 3 weeks post-BMT, known CMV+, HSV+. Acute respiratory illness with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. BAL = 3+ HSV. Name 3 possible causes other than HSV

parts.text: Name 3 possible causes other than HSV.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 possible causes other than HSV

questions.model_answer: a) (1) CMV pneumonitis (reactivation typically at ~3-12 weeks post-transplant in a CMV-seropositive recipient). (2) Community respiratory viral pneumonia – influenza, RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, or human metapneumovirus. (3) Non-infectious diffuse alveolar process – idiopathic pneumonia syndrome / diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. (Detection of HSV in BAL is often colonization/shedding rather than true HSV pneumonia, so an alternative cause should be actively sought; bacterial pneumonia and early invasive aspergillosis are also possible.)

cohort_answer.text: Infectious: bacterial pneumonia, viral pneumonia (influenza, COVID, RSV, parainfluenza), adenovirus, aspergillus, CMV pneumonitis (less likely given timeline). Non-infectious: pulmonary edema, alveolar hemorrhage, ARDS, GVHD, idiopathic pneumonia, organizing pneumonia.

questions.model_answer: a) Start at the beginning of the conditioning regimen. b) Continue at least until engraftment/WBC recovery and resolution of mucositis (approximately day +30); extend (up to ≥1 year) if ongoing GVHD, frequent HSV recurrences, or if concurrent VZV prophylaxis is warranted. c) Acyclovir 400–800 mg PO BID (or IV 5 mg/kg q12h if unable to take oral), or valacyclovir 500 mg PO once to twice daily. d) No. e) Because HSV disease post-transplant is due to reactivation of the recipient's own latent virus in sensory (dorsal root/trigeminal) ganglia; the graft does not transmit latent HSV, so recipient rather than donor serostatus determines prophylaxis.

cohort_answer.text: A) Start of conditioning. B) Ppx until WBC recovery AND mucositis resolution; can be extended to a year if frequent recurrent HSV infections, GVHD, or needs ongoing VZV ppx. C) Acyclovir 400mg PO BID in adults; Valacyclovir 500mg PO daily. D) No. E) HSV is only latent in dorsal root/sensory ganglia.

questions.question: A patient 15 months post bone marrow transplant is exposed to a room-mate with chickenpox.
questions.question_raw: Post BMT patient at 15 months. Exposed to room-mate with chicken pox.

parts.text: What do you do, and what is the period of infectivity for the patient?
What are the vaccines indicated for her at 12 months, assuming she is well with no immune suppression?
When can you give the VZV vaccine for her, and what would be two contraindications at that time?

parts_raw.text: What do you do? Period of infectivity for the patient?
What are the vaccines indicated for her at 12 months assuming well and no immune suppression
When can you give VZV vaccine for her and what would be 2 contraindications at that time?

questions.model_answer:
a) Confirm the diagnosis in the room-mate; isolate the room-mate (airborne + contact). This patient is <24 months post-BMT and remains at high risk, so give VariZIG as soon as possible, up to 10 days after exposure, regardless of prior serostatus. Consider pre-emptive valacyclovir/acyclovir if VariZIG is unavailable; place in airborne isolation during the at-risk window and treat with IV acyclovir if varicella develops. If she becomes infected, she is contagious from ~1-2 days before rash until all lesions have crusted.
b) At 12 months post-BMT (well, not immunosuppressed) give inactivated vaccines per the reconstitution schedule: pneumococcal conjugate series, Hib, tetanus/diphtheria (DTaP/Tdap), inactivated polio, hepatitis B, meningococcal, HPV, and inactivated influenza. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are deferred.
c) Live attenuated varicella/zoster vaccine may be given only >=24 months post-transplant and only if the patient is immunocompetent and free of active GVHD/immunosuppression. Two contraindications at that time: (1) ongoing immunosuppression or active graft-versus-host disease; (2) recent immune globulin/VariZIG or IVIG administration (defer live vaccine), or a hypersensitivity reaction to a vaccine component.
questions.beyond_mandell: Post-HCT vaccine reconstitution schedule and the 24-month live-vaccine deferral are IDSA/CDC/Red Book transplant guidance; this chapter states only that VZV vaccine is a live vaccine and confirms VariZIG use in exposed immunocompromised persons.

cohort_answer.text: A) Confirm diagnosis; incubation 14-16 days (range 10-21); infectivity 24-48h pre-exanthem until all lesions crusted (day 8-21 post-exposure isolation, 28 if VZIG used); confirm vaccine/infection/serologic status; VZV-seronegative HCT recipients transplanted within previous 24 months (or >24 months if continued immunosuppression e.g. chronic GVHD) should get VariZIG within 10 days of contact; seropositive but highly immunosuppressed patients should also get VariZIG; cannot give vaccine post-BMT until at least 2 years; isolate roommate in airborne; isolate BMT patient in airborne from day 8 post-exposure until day 28 (VZIG given). B) Immunize with 2 doses of Shingrix at least 1 year after herpes zoster episode; other vaccines 12 months post-BMT include 3 doses PCV at 3-6 months then PPV-23 at 12-18 months, HiB conjugate 3 doses at 6 months, Td at 6 months, inactivated polio at 6 months, HepB 3 doses at 6 months, HPV 3 doses at 6 months, meningococcal at 6 months, influenza 4-6 months post-transplant; live vaccines (MMR, varicella, YF) at 24 months post-BMT. C) Live attenuated Zostavax: wait 24 months post-transplant; inactivated Shingrix: wait 3-6 months post-transplant. Contraindications: hypersensitivity reaction; ongoing immunosuppression (for GVHD); IVIG (last 8-11 months).

questions.question: RSV infection in a bone marrow (hematopoietic cell) transplant patient. Outline the management.
questions.question_raw: RSV in a BMT patient.

parts.text: Management?

parts_raw.text: Management?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Antiviral therapy with ribavirin — inhaled/aerosolized (2 g over 2-3 h TID intermittently, or 6 g over 18 h continuously) or oral/IV ribavirin, most effective when started while disease is still limited to the upper respiratory tract to prevent progression to lower tract disease; guard against teratogenicity. (2) Adjunctive immunoglobulin (IVIG) or anti-F monoclonal antibody (palivizumab) may be added in highly immunocompromised patients, though evidence is retrospective. (3) Supportive care (oxygen, hydration, respiratory support) plus strict infection-control/isolation to prevent nosocomial spread, with early diagnosis and screening on transplant units.

cohort_answer.text: Oral Ribavirin 15-20mg/kg/day divided TID x10 days; toxicities include teratogenicity (long t1/2), hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, cough/dyspnea/bronchoconstriction, neuropsychologic symptoms; can also consider IVIG and palivizumab.

questions.question: List four vaccines contraindicated in the first year after bone marrow transplant.

parts.text: List four vaccines contraindicated in the first year post-bone marrow transplant.

parts_raw.text: List 4 vaccines contraindicated in the first year post-BMT

questions.model_answer: Any live vaccine is contraindicated in the first year (and generally until 24 months) after HSCT: (1) Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR). (2) Varicella vaccine (and live zoster vaccine, Zostavax). (3) Live attenuated influenza vaccine (intranasal) — inactivated influenza vaccine is used instead. (4) BCG. Also contraindicated: oral rotavirus vaccine, yellow fever, oral typhoid (Ty21a), live attenuated Japanese encephalitis and oral polio vaccine. Note that recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is non-live and is recommended, and may be given from about 3–6 months post-transplant.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI/AST: recombinant zoster vaccine is the preferred non-live alternative to live zoster vaccine post-HSCT.

cohort_answer.text: Any 4 live vaccines: MMR, Varicella vaccine, live HZ vaccine (Zostavax), Rotavirus, Yellow fever, live Japanese encephalitis vaccine, BCG, live influenza vaccine.

questions.question: A patient is two years post-transplant and it is November.
questions.question_raw: In a patient 2 years post-transplant (it is November)

parts.text: Give a reason not to vaccinate.
Name two vaccines that are a priority for household members.

parts_raw.text: A reason not to vaccinate?
2 vaccines that are a priority for household members?

questions.model_answer:
a) Ongoing significant immunosuppression — active chronic GVHD requiring systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapy. Such a patient is unlikely to mount a protective response, and live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella) remain contraindicated until off immunosuppression and free of GVHD. Recent receipt of IVIG or other antibody-containing blood product is a further reason to defer live measles- and varicella-containing vaccines, for 8 to 11 months depending on the product and dose.

b) Given it is November: (1) Inactivated influenza vaccine, annually, for all household members and close contacts — the single highest-yield cocoon strategy. (2) COVID-19 vaccine, up to date. Other priorities: MMR and varicella for non-immune household members (these live vaccines are safe for contacts, as vaccine virus is not transmitted, except for rare varicella-vaccine rash — cover the rash and avoid contact if it occurs), Tdap for pertussis, and rotavirus for infants in the household (with hand hygiene, as vaccine virus is shed in stool for up to 4 weeks). Household contacts should not receive live attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine or oral polio vaccine if the transplant recipient is severely immunocompromised.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI Immunization of Immunocompromised Persons: cocooning with inactivated influenza and COVID-19 vaccine; LAIV avoided in contacts of severely immunocompromised patients.

cohort_answer.text: A) If patient still immunosuppressed + GVHD, may not respond to vaccines and live attenuated vaccines contraindicated; current/recent IVIG administration (lack of vaccine efficacy) in the last 8-11 months. B) Household members should prioritize transmissible vaccine-preventable diseases: flu, Hep A/B, Pneumococcus, Pertussis, HiB, Rotavirus, MMRV, Zoster (also note MMRV vaccine viruses not transmitted to contacts; zoster and vaccinia rare shedding; rotavirus sheds in stool up to 4 weeks).

questions.question: Describe your approach to vaccination over the first 2 years post-bone marrow (hematopoietic stem cell) transplant.
questions.question_raw: Describe your approach to vaccination over the first 2 years post-BMT?

parts.text: Approach to vaccination over the first 2 years post-bone marrow transplant

parts_raw.text: Approach to vaccination over first 2 years post-BMT

questions.model_answer: a) Principle: myeloablation destroys pre-existing immune memory, so all recipients (autologous and allogeneic alike) are treated as never immunized and given a full primary re-immunization series; responses to polysaccharide antigens are poor, so conjugate vaccines are preferred and serology may be checked where available. Pre-transplant, if time permits: age-appropriate inactivated vaccines, conjugate pneumococcal vaccine regardless of age, and inactivated influenza in season, given at least 2 weeks before conditioning; no live vaccine within 4 weeks of starting conditioning. Post-transplant inactivated schedule: inactivated influenza annually starting 4-6 months post-transplant (lifelong); conjugate pneumococcal 3-dose primary series starting 3-6 months, doses at least 4 weeks apart, with a booster at 12-18 months (a polysaccharide or additional conjugate dose at 12-18 months depending on product); diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (age-appropriate DTaP/Tdap) 3 doses from 6-12 months; Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate 3 doses from 6-12 months; inactivated polio 3 doses from 6-12 months; hepatitis B 3-4 doses from 6-12 months using high-dose/double-dose product with post-series serology; quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate 2 doses from 6-12 months (and meningococcal B, particularly with GVHD, asplenia, or eculizumab); HPV 3-dose series from 6-12 months in eligible ages; consider hepatitis A, and household/close-contact immunization (cocooning) with inactivated influenza and Tdap. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are deferred to 24 months post-transplant and given only if there is no chronic GVHD, immunosuppression has been stopped for more than 3 months, malignancy is in remission, and there is evidence of immune reconstitution; zoster live vaccine is avoided (use recombinant subunit instead). If the patient is receiving IVIG, delay measles- and varicella-containing vaccines by 8-11 months after the last dose. Yellow fever may be considered after 24 months in a reconstituted, non-immunosuppressed traveller to an endemic area. Antimicrobial prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms continues alongside vaccination while immunosuppressed.
questions.beyond_mandell: Schedule follows NACI/CIC Canadian Immunization Guide immunocompromised chapter and IDSA/ASBMT 2013 guidelines for HSCT recipients.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-HSCT: if time permits, give all routine inactivated vaccines appropriate for age, conjugate pneumococcal vaccine regardless of age (ideally Pneu-C-20), polysaccharide pneumococcal if age ≥2 + Pneu-C-13/15, inactivated influenza if flu season; give inactivated vaccines ≥2 weeks before transplant; live vaccines not within 4 weeks of conditioning start. Post-HSCT: treat allogeneic same as autologous; consider all as never immunized and re-immunize (bone marrow ablation eliminates immune memory); poor response to polysaccharide vaccines; measure post-vaccination titres if possible; higher risk for pneumococcus, Hib, measles, varicella, influenza. Schedule: DTP 3 doses from 6-12 months post-HSCT; Hib 3 doses from 6-12 months; HepB 3-4 doses at 6-12 months (double dose); HPV 3 doses at 6-12 months; influenza (inactivated) annually from 4-6 months; quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate 2 doses from 6 months (if asplenic); PNEU-C-20 primary series 3 doses starting 3-9 months (≥4 weeks apart) + booster at 12-18 months; inactivated polio 3 doses at 6-12 months. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) at 24 months post-BMT if no GVHD, immunosuppression stopped >3 months, disease inactive, and immunocompetent; YF vaccine possible if criteria met and travelling to endemic area; IVIG inactivates live vaccines so delay 8-11 months after last IVIG dose.

questions.question: A patient is post-hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) and develops CMV DNAemia.
questions.question_raw: Post HSCT and develops CMV DNAemia.

parts.text: What are 5 risk factors for CMV disease?
Define pre-emptive and prophylaxis strategies (describe each, no advantages/disadvantages).
How is IV ganciclovir metabolized, and when might the dose need adjusting?
For resistant CMV disease, name three antivirals that may be considered for a UL97 mutation and one for a UL54 mutation.

parts_raw.text: What are 5 risk factors for CMV disease
Define pre-emptive and prophylaxis strategies (no advantages/disadvantages, just describe)
How is IV ganciclovir metabolized, and when might the dose need adjusting
For resistant CMV disease, name three antivirals that may be considered for UL97 mutation and one for UL54 mutation.

questions.model_answer:
a) Five risk factors for CMV disease after HSCT: (1) Recipient CMV-seropositive status (D+/R+ or D-/R+ = high risk in HSCT). (2) HLA mismatch (related donor with one HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch, or unrelated donor with one HLA-A/-B/-C/-DR mismatch). (3) Use of T-lymphocyte-depleting strategies (antithymocyte globulin or alemtuzumab). (4) Umbilical-cord-blood HSCT into a seropositive recipient, or HLA-haploidentical HSCT. (5) Graft-versus-host disease requiring steroid therapy.
b) Pre-emptive therapy: serial quantitative virologic monitoring of blood/body fluids for CMV replication, with antiviral therapy initiated only once a predetermined viral threshold is reached, continued until the infection resolves or the viral load falls substantially. Prophylaxis: administration of antiviral drug to all at-risk patients from early post-transplant regardless of viral load, to prevent infection (often followed by a pre-emptive strategy once prophylaxis stops).
c) Ganciclovir is not appreciably metabolized; it is excreted almost unchanged in the urine (intracellularly it is phosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase then by host kinases to the active triphosphate, but the drug itself undergoes renal, not hepatic, clearance). Therefore the dose must be adjusted according to renal function (renal impairment/dialysis).
d) UL97 mutation (confers ganciclovir resistance; virus remains susceptible to other-target agents): (1) Foscarnet, (2) Cidofovir, (3) Maribavir (a UL97 kinase inhibitor active against GCV-resistant virus). UL54 (DNA polymerase) mutation, which confers cross-resistance to ganciclovir, cidofovir and foscarnet: Maribavir (acts on UL97, not the polymerase).

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: CMV seropositivity (D-/R+); T cell depletion (ATG); GVHD; Immunosuppressive drugs (steroids, alemtuzumab); Lymphopenia. Pre-emptive therapy: Patients monitored frequently (weekly) with CMV load and antiviral therapy initiated when viral replication reaches a certain assay threshold defined at each institution. Prophylaxis: Immediate start of prophylaxis (ganciclovir, valganciclovir, letermovir) post-transplant in high risk patients. Ganciclovir metabolism: Acyclic analog of nucleoside guanosine, converted intracellularly to ganciclovir 5'-monophosphate by viral kinase encoded by CMV gene UL97 during infection; cellular kinases catalyze formation of ganciclovir diphosphate and triphosphate (10-fold greater concentration in CMV infected cells); ganciclovir triphosphate is a competitive inhibitor of dGTP incorporation into DNA, preferentially inhibiting viral DNA polymerases, and is a poor substrate for chain elongation, disrupting viral DNA synthesis. Dose adjustment needed: Renal impairment; Dialysis; Pre-emptive therapy (induction 5mg/kg q12 vs maintenance 5mg/kg q24); UL97 mutation for <5x (10mg/kg q12, off-label); Intravitreal injection (off-label). Resistant CMV: UL97 mutation - Foscarnet, Cidofovir, Maribavir, possibly high dose ganciclovir. UL54 mutation - Maribavir, Foscarnet (avoid cidofovir)

questions.question: In patients with high-risk neutropenia, describe the advantages and disadvantages of preemptive (diagnostic-driven) antifungal prophylaxis compared with empirical antifungal therapy for invasive fungal infection.
questions.question_raw: 26. In patients with high risk neutropenia, describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

parts.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

parts_raw.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

questions.model_answer: a) Advantages: (1) Less antifungal drug use, avoiding the marked overtreatment inherent in empirical therapy (which treats fever alone), with reduced cost, lower toxicity, and less selection pressure for resistant fungi. (2) No increase in overall mortality compared with the empirical approach, so IFD outcomes are not compromised by the more restrained strategy. Disadvantages: (1) More invasive fungal infections are detected/occur in the diagnostic-driven arm, and non-inferiority for survival was not demonstrated in the highest-risk first-remission-induction subgroup. (2) It depends on resource-heavy diagnostics: readily available thin-slice chest CT with skilled radiologists, reliable galactomannan/antigen assays with 2-3 day turnaround, and its reliability falls when mold-active prophylaxis lowers galactomannan sensitivity/specificity.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-emptive often involves serial HRCT and Galactomannan/B-D-Glucan. Advantages: Decreased costs of antifungal drugs; lower risk of resistance; minimises risk of drug related toxicity. Disadvantages: Requires frequent testing; delayed start of therapy; higher rates of invasive fungal infection.

What are 2 antivirals from different classes that can be used for treatment?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Myeloablative conditioning regimen. (2) Graft-versus-host disease (immune reconstitution). (3) Allogeneic (vs autologous) graft. (4) HLA-mismatched/unrelated donor graft (also BKV seropositivity, older age). b) Urine BKV DNA PCR (viruria); urine cytology for decoy cells is an adjunct. c) Intravesical/IV cidofovir (nucleotide analog) and a fluoroquinolone - ciprofloxacin (inhibits BKV-encoded DNA gyrase; prophylaxis reduces post-HSCT hemorrhagic cystitis).
questions.beyond_mandell: Naming ciprofloxacin/cidofovir as being from different drug classes reflects standard classification; the chapter presents both agents but does not frame them as a two-drug regimen.

questions.question: A patient with autologous stem cell transplant develops BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis.
questions.question_raw: Q72 2023 Day 1. AutoSCT with BK hemorrhagic cystitis. (VIRUSES)

parts.text: Four risk factors.
One urinary test to diagnose, in addition to her symptoms.
Which 2 antiviral drugs to treat.

parts_raw.text: 4 risk factors
One urinary test to diagnose, in addition to her symptoms
Which 2 antiviral drugs to treat

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Myeloablative conditioning regimen. (2) Graft-versus-host disease. (3) Allogeneic graft (hemorrhagic cystitis rarely seen in autologous recipients). (4) HLA-mismatched/unrelated donor graft (also BKV seropositivity, older age). b) Urine BKV DNA PCR (viruria) - increased urine viral load with hematuria supports the diagnosis. c) Cidofovir (intravesical or IV) and ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone).
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter notes BKV hemorrhagic cystitis is characteristically an allogeneic (not autologous) HSCT complication; treatment evidence for cidofovir/ciprofloxacin is limited to case series and small retrospective studies.

cohort_answer.text:
4 risk factors: Myeloablative conditioning regimens (HLA mismatch higher risk); haploidentical donor; GVHD (acute and chronic); CMV reactivation; male sex.
Urinary test/symptoms: Typically BK viruria; BKPyV serum can help with diagnosis; BK viremia >10,000 copies/mL more likely to occur; symptoms - cystitis (dysuria, urgency, abdominal pain), hematuria, AKI.
2 antiviral drugs: Intravesicular and IV Cidofovir (no RCT data, some observational studies); Brincidofovir (pro-drug of Cidofovir); Leflunomide (has some antiviral properties against BKV).

questions.question: Vaccines in hematopoietic stem cell transplant and solid organ transplant patients.
questions.question_raw: Vaccines in HSCT/SOT transplant patients

parts.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines post-transplant?

parts_raw.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines post-transplant?

questions.model_answer:
a) Inactivated vaccines should be given at least 2 weeks before transplant (before the start of conditioning for HSCT, or before transplant/induction immunosuppression for SOT), so that the response is mounted while the patient is still relatively immunocompetent. Live vaccines require a longer interval — at least 4 weeks before conditioning or transplant. Ideally the full indicated schedule is completed during the pre-transplant assessment, as immunogenicity is much better before than after transplant.

b) HSCT: inactivated vaccines are restarted at 3 to 6 months post-transplant — influenza vaccine as early as 3–4 months (or 6 months, with a second dose if given earlier), and the routine re-immunization series (pneumococcal conjugate, Tdap-IPV-Hib, hepatitis B, meningococcal, HPV) generally beginning at 6 months. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are deferred to at least 24 months post-transplant and only if the patient is off immunosuppression, free of chronic GVHD, and immunocompetent. SOT: inactivated vaccines are given from 3 to 6 months post-transplant, once maintenance-level immunosuppression is reached and the patient is stable; influenza vaccine may be given as early as 1 month post-transplant during an outbreak or season. Live vaccines are generally contraindicated after SOT. Additional points: hepatitis B at double dose with serologic follow-up, HPV as a 3-dose series regardless of age, and recombinant zoster vaccine (non-live) is safe and indicated in both populations.
questions.beyond_mandell: AST Infectious Diseases Community of Practice vaccination guidelines and NACI Immunization of Immunocompromised Persons.

cohort_answer.text: A) Inactivated vaccines: at least 2 weeks before conditioning. Live attenuated vaccines: at least 4 weeks before conditioning. B) SOT: live vaccines not recommended post-SOT; inactivated vaccine wait 3-6 months post-transplant or when maintenance immunosuppression attained; HepB at double usual dose; HPV 3-dose schedule regardless of age. HSCT: live vaccine around 24 months post-transplant if immunocompetent and no GVHD; inactivated vaccine 6-12 months post-transplant; COVID (3 doses + boosters) can begin 3-6 months post-transplant.
